section.title: A Cry Against Lying Lips
section.sectionRationale: This is the first of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the great feasts, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. It is an individual lament, the opening cry of the pilgrim road, voiced from a place of slander and hostility farthest from Zion.
section.thesis: Surrounded by lying lips and people who hate peace, the psalmist cries to the LORD who answers, and even while he longs only for peace, he trusts God to deal with deceit rather than answering war with war.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the cry for deliverance from a deceitful tongue and its certain judgment, verses 1 to 4, and the lament of dwelling among those who want war, verses 5 to 7.

units.label: In my distress I cried to the LORD

verses.text: In my {{tsarah|distress}} I cried to the LORD, and He answered me.
Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue.
What will He do to you, and what will be added to you, O deceitful tongue?
Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree!

units.label: Too long have I dwelt among war
units.note: the ache of exile among the hostile

verses.text: Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!
Too long have I dwelt among those who hate {{shalom|peace}}.
I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war.

tsarah.gloss: Distress, a tight or cramped place. The psalmist's trouble is pictured as confinement, and his cry is the instinct of the pressed soul turning to the LORD first.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being, not merely the absence of conflict. The psalmist longs for shalom even while living among those who hate it and want war instead.

basic.context: This psalm opens the fifteen Songs of Ascents, sung by pilgrims climbing toward Jerusalem for the three annual feasts. It begins the journey from the farthest point, a place of slander and hostility, crying out to the LORD before the pilgrim road even begins to climb.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes a real experience of being lied about and surrounded by people who want war, and it prescribes the abiding pattern of crying to the LORD first and continuing to seek peace rather than repaying evil with evil.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist's trouble is tsarah, a tight, cramped distress, and his cry is answered. He closes longing for shalom, peace and wholeness, even while those around him hate it and choose war.
basic.typology: The psalmist's plea against lying lips anticipates Christ, who endured false witnesses at His trial and did not revile in return, entrusting Himself to the One who judges justly.
basic.christ: Jesus is the greater pilgrim who set His face to go to Jerusalem though it meant false accusation and the cross, and He Himself is our peace, breaking down the hostility this psalm laments.
basic.god: God is the one who answers the distressed cry, and He is trusted to deal justly with deceitful and warlike tongues in His own time and way.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 2:23 shows Christ entrusting Himself to the just Judge rather than reviling in return. Matthew 26:59 to 60 records false witnesses seeking Jesus' destruction. Ephesians 2:14 names Christ Himself as our peace. James 3:5 to 6 describes the tongue's destructive fire.
basic.oneStory: This opening Song of Ascents cries out from the far country of deceit and hostility, the first step of a pilgrim road that climbs, psalm by psalm, toward the peace of Zion fulfilled in Christ.

context.literary:
Psalm 120 is short, but it has a clear four-part shape. Verse 1 is a testimony in the past: the speaker cried and was answered. Verse 2 is the present prayer that grows out of it, a request to be rescued from lying lips. Verses 3 and 4 turn on the liar himself and ask him directly what he can expect, with a blunt answer in verse 4. Verses 5 to 7 are lament, a sigh of weariness from a man living in the wrong place among the wrong people.

The poem is held together by the sounds and subjects of speech. Lips and tongue appear in verses 2 and 3, and the speaker's own speech appears in verse 7: 'when I speak, they want war.' The psalm is about words, those that lie and those that offer peace, and the speaker's cry in verse 1 is itself a speech that God answers.

The first line sets a pattern for the rest of the collection. The pilgrim does not first describe his enemies; he reports that he cried and was heard. Most later Songs of Ascents also begin in the middle of a story of trouble and rescue, and they teach their singers to carry that story up the road. The psalm is also the only one of the fifteen that ends in a war. The others move to Zion and to peace, and this one starts as far from either as it is possible to be.

The verses 3 and 4 are the poem's central turn. The question 'What will He do to you, and what will be added to you?' has the sound of an oath formula, and compares with the form of curse in 1 Samuel 3:17, 'May God punish you, and ever so severely.' The poet does not curse in his own voice. He lets God's answer be seen in the sharp arrows and the burning coals, so that the deceiver is warned and the speaker leaves the matter with the Judge.
context.historical:
The title marks this as the first of fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134. The meaning of 'ascents' is debated, as the discussion below shows, but the most natural setting is the pilgrim climb to Jerusalem, which sits high in the hill country and could only be reached by going up. Later Jewish tradition connected the fifteen psalms with fifteen steps in the temple, and the pilgrim feasts were the occasions when large crowds sang on the road.

Meshech and Kedar belong to different worlds. Meshech is listed among the sons of Japheth, Genesis 10:2, and in Ezekiel 27:13 it appears with Javan and Tubal as a trading nation that dealt in slaves and bronze utensils, far to the north of Israel. Kedar is one of the sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13, a nomadic Arabian people whose black tents are used for comparison in Song of Songs 1:5, and whose glory is said to be doomed in Isaiah 21:16 to 17 and Jeremiah 49:28. Both are known to Israel as foreign, and neither was a place an Israelite lived by choice.

It would be easy to push a literal reading too far. A man cannot have lived in both places at once, and the psalm says 'tents' of Kedar and 'dwell' in Meshech as a figure of speech for living among people who are foreign to the life of the covenant. Israelites in the dispersion, or merchants, or exiles, would have recognised the experience.

The broom tree in verse 4 is a desert shrub whose wood the ancients used for fuel, and it was known for burning hotly. The arrows of the warrior and the coals of broom wood make a picture from desert and battle, which suits a speaker who is in the tents of Kedar, whether near or far.
context.canonical:
Psalm 120 is the doorway to a collection, and the collection gives it meaning. The fifteen songs begin with a cry from the far country and end in Psalm 134 with servants of the LORD who 'serve by night in the house of the LORD,' and who are told, 'May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion,' Psalm 134:1 to 3. The climb from the first to the last is a climb from distress to blessing.

In that journey the word 'peace' becomes the theme that answers this psalm's complaint. Psalm 120:7 ends with a man of peace faced by people who want war. Psalm 122:6 to 8 then calls the pilgrims to 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem' and says the word peace three times, and Psalm 125:5 and 128:6 close with 'Peace be upon Israel.' The pilgrim who left the place of war arrives at a city whose name means peace.

The subject of the deceitful tongue is also a long one in Scripture. The Proverbs list lying lips and false witness among the things the LORD hates, Proverbs 6:16 to 19 and 12:22. Psalm 52:2 to 4 and Psalm 140:3 describe the tongue as a razor and as the venom of vipers, and Jeremiah 9:3 says people 'bend their tongues like bows.' James 3:5 to 6 describes the tongue as a fire.

And in the New Testament the figure of the one who is slandered and does not repay becomes the pattern. Peter says of Jesus that 'when they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. Paul's counsel in Romans 12:17 to 21, 'Do not repay anyone evil for evil,' and 'live at peace with everyone,' is the practical form of the psalmist's decision in verse 7 to be for peace.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written to teach a pilgrim people what to do with the pain of living among people who lie and fight. Its answer is a sequence. First cry out to the LORD, and remember that he has answered before, verse 1. Then ask for rescue, not revenge, verse 2. Then leave the liar to a justice that is not your own, verses 3 and 4. Then admit honestly how tiring it is, verses 5 and 6, and hold on to peace as your own choice even when no one else wants it, verse 7.

The writer also meant the pilgrims to hear this at the start of their journey. They were about to leave home and travel up to Jerusalem, and the first thing the song does is to name what they are leaving, a world in which the neighbours are hostile and truth is cheap. The first song in the collection is a song of departure from a bad place as much as one of arrival at a good one.

It is also a psalm about the cost of being a peacemaker. The speaker is not a quiet man avoiding conflict but a man whose speech for peace provokes war. The writer wants those who sing it to know that to seek peace may bring hostility, and that God hears the one who does it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a man's distress and his wish that the deceitful tongue meet a fiery end. The sharp arrows and burning coals in verse 4 are a statement of what God will do, not a command to the pilgrim to do it. Reading the poem as a licence for a believer to take revenge would reverse its direction, since the speaker brings his case to the LORD and does not draw a weapon himself.

The psalm does not prescribe that a believer must stay in a hostile environment, or must leave it. It reports that the speaker has lived too long among those who hate peace, verse 6, and its answer is to cry to the LORD and be for peace, not to specify a place to live. What carries over is the order: pray first, ask for deliverance, leave judgment with God, and keep one's own speech peaceable.

Christians are told something very close in Romans 12:18 to 21: live at peace as far as it depends on you, do not avenge yourselves, leave room for God's wrath, and overcome evil with good. The psalm gives the emotional reality that sits under that teaching, which is that peacemaking is tiring, that it is not always received, and that it is carried out in prayer.

debates.question: Are Meshech and Kedar literal locations or figures for hostile exile?

views.label: Literal distant peoples
views.case: Meshech, in Asia Minor, and Kedar, an Arabian tribe, are real and famously hostile peoples, so the psalmist may genuinely have sojourned among them.

views.label: Figurative language for hostility
views.case: Since the two lie at opposite ends of the map, north and south, they are more likely paired as a figure of speech for any place of exile among those who hate peace.

debates.bearing: Either way, the psalm voices the ache of living, literally or figuratively, far from God's peace among people bent on conflict.

debates.question: What does 'ascents' mean in the title Song of Ascents?

views.label: The pilgrim climb to Jerusalem
views.case: The most common view takes the fifteen psalms as songs for pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the feasts. Psalm 122:1 to 2 speaks of going to the house of the LORD and standing in the gates, and Psalm 121 looks at the hills ahead.

views.label: The return from exile
views.case: Ezra 7:9 uses the same word for the journey from Babylon, and the collection includes psalms about restoration and Zion, such as Psalm 126, so some read the ascents as the great ascent of the returning exiles.

views.label: The temple steps or a rising melody
views.case: Later Jewish tradition links the songs with the fifteen steps of the temple, where Levites sang, and some suggest a musical form in which each line takes up the last words of the one before.

debates.bearing: These readings are compatible. The songs may have been written for pilgrims, used on the return and later sung at the temple. For this psalm, the 'ascent' begins in the far country, so that the whole climb is understood as a journey out of hostility toward peace.

debates.question: Who speaks the words of verse 4?

views.label: God, answering the deceitful tongue
views.case: The nearest antecedent of the 'He' in verse 3 is God, and the sharp arrows and burning coals are what the judge will send. This is the reading the BSB's wording supports.

views.label: The psalmist, calling down judgment
views.case: Some take verse 4 as the speaker's own imprecation, similar to Psalm 140:9 to 10, which prays that burning coals fall on enemies.

debates.bearing: Both readings leave the weapon in God's hand. Whether the poet states what God will do or prays for it, he does not himself draw an arrow, and the next verses return to his own weariness.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm begins with a verb in the perfect, 'I cried,' qarati, and a reply that follows it, 'and He answered me,' so the opening is the report of a past rescue. The tense invites two readings, and both are probably meant. It may recall an earlier occasion that supplies the confidence for the request in verse 2, or it may declare that the answer came in the very act of crying. Either way, the prayer rests on something God has already done.

The prayer in verse 2 asks God to 'deliver,' hatsilah, the verb for pulling something out of danger, and what is to be delivered is the nephesh, here rendered 'soul.' The word means the whole self, the life that can be harmed by words. The same word appears again in verse 6, 'Too long have I dwelt,' which is literally 'much has my soul dwelt.' The psalm brackets its complaint with the nephesh: it is the whole person, not a mere reputation, that has been under siege.

The liars have 'lying lips,' sifte sheqer, where sheqer is the common word for falsehood, as in the ninth commandment's 'false testimony,' Exodus 20:16. The 'deceitful tongue,' lashon remiyyah, adds a second word, remiyyah, whose sense is treachery or slackness, and which Hosea 7:16 and Psalm 78:57 use in the phrase about a bow that fails the archer. The reader may hear in it a tongue that fails the one who trusts it. The tongue is trained, shot and burnt in the same poem, since in verse 4 the arrows follow it.

Verse 3 has two verbs in the formula 'give' and 'add,' and the question 'What will He do to you, and what will be added to you?' reflects an oath formula in which a person calls down more on himself if he lies. The liar who swears falsely is told what will in fact be added to him.

In verse 4 the coals are from the retem, the broom tree, sometimes translated juniper. It is a desert shrub, and its wood was often said to burn long and hot, so the picture is of a penalty that does not die quickly.

Verse 5 begins with an exclamation, 'Woe to me,' oyah li, and the verb for dwelling in Meshech is gur, which means to live as a stranger or sojourner. It is the word for the ger, the resident alien, and Psalm 119:19 uses its form for the psalmist who is a stranger on the earth. The psalmist is a resident alien among the tents of Kedar.

The last verse is spare in Hebrew: ani shalom, which is literally 'I am peace.' English must supply 'I am in favor of.' The next words are 'but when I speak, they are for war,' where 'war,' milchamah, stands against 'peace,' shalom. The two nouns put the whole psalm in a line: one man whose very being is peace, and a crowd whose answer to peace is war.

typology.type: The one slandered by lying lips, verses 2 to 3
typology.fulfillment: The speaker is attacked by lying lips and a deceitful tongue, and he turns to the LORD. At His trial Jesus was met by those who 'were seeking false testimony against Jesus in order to put Him to death,' Matthew 26:59, and, as Mark puts it, 'their testimony was inconsistent,' Mark 14:56. He answered the lies with silence, Mark 14:61, in line with Isaiah 53:7, and 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. The correspondence is that of the innocent man accused by liars. The type falls short because the psalmist can only ask for rescue, but Jesus's false conviction and death become the means of rescuing the very people who accused Him.

typology.type: The pilgrim far from peace, verses 5 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The speaker lives among strangers who hate peace and longs for it. Jesus too lived among those who did not receive Him, John 1:11, and said 'My peace I give to you,' John 14:27. He wept over Jerusalem, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace,' Luke 19:41 to 42. Ephesians says He 'preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' Ephesians 2:17, so that the far-off ones are brought home. The correspondence is that the far country is crossed. The type falls short because the psalmist is carried by the pilgrim road, while Christ Himself is the peace and makes it by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20.

typology.type: The man of peace met with war, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: 'I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war' sums up the ministry of Jesus. He is announced as the one who brings 'peace on earth,' Luke 2:14, and called Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6, yet He was opposed and put to death. His disciples are told 'Blessed are the peacemakers,' Matthew 5:9, and promised that they will be insulted and slandered, Matthew 5:11. The correspondence is that peace brings opposition. The type falls short because the psalmist's peace is only his own wish, whereas Christ makes peace between God and people, Romans 5:1, and the conflict ends in reconciliation.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first as the pattern of the righteous man slandered. The speaker's request to be delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue was fulfilled in an extreme form at the trial of Jesus, when the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin sought false testimony against him, Matthew 26:59 to 60, and many gave it, though their stories did not agree, Mark 14:56. Peter's summary of how Jesus bore it is the closest New Testament echo: 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. That is the psalm's order of response, a cry to God and a refusal of revenge, lived out at the cross. Isaiah had said of the servant that 'nor was any deceit in His mouth,' Isaiah 53:9, which is the reverse of the deceitful tongue.

It leads to Christ as the true man of peace. The line 'I am for peace' is the line of one whose very person is peace. Isaiah called the promised child the Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6, the angels sang of peace on earth, Luke 2:14, and Paul says plainly that 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14. He did not simply wish for peace; He came to those far off and made it, 'by making peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20. The people whose answer to peace was war were the ones for whom He made it.

It leads to Christ as the pilgrim. The first Song of Ascents begins the road that the Gospel of Luke describes when it says that Jesus 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem,' Luke 9:51. He went up to the city whose name means peace, and He went into the heart of the hostility the psalmist describes. He also wept over it, saying that it had missed what would bring it peace, Luke 19:41 to 42.

It leads to Christ in the blessing He promises to those who follow Him. The psalmist's experience of being hated for wanting peace is picked up in the Beatitudes, where Jesus says that peacemakers will be called sons of God and those who are slandered because of Him are blessed, Matthew 5:9 and 11.

A caution is needed. The psalm is not a coded prophecy of the trial, and the arrows and coals of verse 4 are not a prediction of anything in the life of Jesus. The link is by pattern. The New Testament itself draws the connection through the experiences of the righteous sufferer and the peace Christ brings, and those are what the psalm supplies.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm says about God is that he answers. It places this before any complaint, in the first line, and it stays true after the complaint. God is the one to whom a person in the far country may cry, and his hearing does not depend on location. A man in the tents of Kedar, who cannot get to the temple, prays all the same and is heard. That gives the whole collection a quiet foundation: the journey toward God's house is made by a people who already know the God of the house.

God is the defender of truth. The psalm sets lying lips against the LORD and trusts him to deal with them. Scripture says the LORD hates a lying tongue and false witness, Proverbs 6:16 to 19, and detests lying lips, Proverbs 12:22. A God who loves truth is not indifferent to its destruction by the tongue. The psalm asks for rescue from lies because God is the God of truth, and the devil, as Jesus says, is the father of lies, John 8:44.

God is a just judge who acts with measured force. The imagery of the warrior's arrows and the broom-wood coals in verse 4 pictures a judgment that is swift and hot and lasts. The poem does not ask the speaker to administer it. This is a God who takes the place of the avenger, as Paul would later say, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' Romans 12:19. The tension in the psalm is that the judgment has not yet fallen as the poem ends, and the speaker is still waiting among those who want war. God's justice is certain and patient, and the believer must live between the cry and the verdict.

God is the source of peace. The psalm places peace in the speaker's mouth, but its source is plainly God, since the pilgrim collection ends with the peace of Jerusalem and the blessing of Zion. The man of peace is a reflection of the God of peace.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to begin with the story of what the LORD has done, to bring what troubles us in plain words, and to keep a desire for peace in a world that does not share it. It is a song for the ones who are tired of a long stay in the wrong place and have not stopped asking, and it assures them that the one they ask is listening.

crossReferences.note: The same pairing of distress and answer appears here with a different word. In 118:5 the speaker cries from the strait and is answered in the wide place, while here the cry is from distress and the rescue is only just beginning. The two psalms together show the arc of a pilgrim from tightness to room.

Kedar is the second son of Ishmael, so the people of Kedar are the desert kin of Abraham's family, living as nomads. The psalmist's complaint that he lives among the tents of Kedar means that he is among people who are close in descent but far from the covenant.

Isaiah foretells that within a year all the glory of Kedar will be gone and its archers will be few. Kedar is famed for its warriors, which fits a psalm that names a people of war, and the prophecy shows that the LORD is the one who humbles them.

Meshech, with Javan and Tubal, traded slaves and bronze with Tyre. It stands for a distant and commercial foreign power, so the psalmist's mention of Meshech evokes a place of foreign trade and foreign values.

Among the things the LORD hates are a lying tongue and a false witness. The list shows that the psalmist's plea against lying lips is not only a private grievance but concerns something God himself abhors.

David describes the deceitful tongue as a sharpened razor and a word that devours. The close wording, 'O deceitful tongue,' places Psalm 120:3 within a family of prayers about slander, in which God is the one who brings the tongue's work to nothing.

The pilgrims arrive and are told to pray for the peace of Jerusalem, with the word peace repeated three times. This is the answer to the speaker of Psalm 120, who lived among those who hate peace, and shows the direction the collection moves.

Paul's instruction not to repay evil for evil, to live at peace as far as possible, and to leave vengeance to God is the pastoral form of what the psalmist does in verses 2 to 4 and 7. It shows how the Psalm is meant to be lived.

Christ, abused, did not retaliate but entrusted himself to the just judge. It is the closest New Testament parallel to the psalm's decision to give the liar to God, and it shows that Jesus took the psalm's path.

The Sanhedrin sought false testimony against Jesus, and many false witnesses came forward. The lying lips that the psalmist feared are given a face here, and the one they accuse is the one who will make peace.

Christ is our peace, has broken down the wall of hostility, and preached peace to those far away and those near. This answers the pilgrim who lived far off among those who wanted war, because the far country has been crossed by the Prince of Peace.

James calls the tongue a fire, a small spark that sets a great forest ablaze. It carries the psalm's concern about the tongue's power into the life of the church, and it shows that the burning coals of verse 4 have a counterpart in the fire a deceitful tongue lights.

study.oneStory:
The first Song of Ascents begins the great journey of the Bible, which is the journey home. Humanity was driven east from the garden, away from God's presence, Genesis 3:24, and the Old Testament's story from then on is one of wandering. Cain settled in the land of Nod, Abraham was told to leave his country, Israel lived as slaves in Egypt and as exiles in Babylon. The speaker of Psalm 120 is one more member of this people, a sojourner in a foreign land who has no peace and knows it.

The lies of the deceitful tongue take us back to the beginning too. The serpent's first move was a lie about what God had said, Genesis 3:4, and Jesus calls the devil the father of lies, John 8:44. Where lies rule, peace is impossible, because trust is gone. The psalm is thus a small picture of life in a fallen world: false words, hostile neighbours, and a longing for a place where truth and peace live together.

In the middle of the Bible's story the road of the pilgrim turns toward a person. The Songs of Ascents climb to Zion, but they cannot themselves make the people fit for it. Jesus, the Prince of Peace, goes up to Jerusalem, is met by false witnesses and by those who prefer war, and makes peace by his death, Colossians 1:20. In him the far-off ones are brought near, Ephesians 2:17, and those who believe 'have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1.

The story ends with the pilgrim finally at home. The city is the one the book of Hebrews calls 'Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22, and Revelation describes the place where there is 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. There the deceitful tongue is silent, since nothing false can enter, Revelation 21:27, and the man of peace is among a people who share it. The psalm's sigh, 'Too long have I dwelt,' is the cry of every pilgrim, and the story of the Bible is God's answer to it.

sermon.title: A Pilgrim's Journey
sermon.why: Begg works through Psalms 120 to 122 together as the launch of the pilgrim's ascent, showing how the cry against lying lips and the longing for peace begins the journey toward the LORD's help and presence in Zion.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask the LORD to deliver him from?

options.text: Lying lips and a deceitful tongue.
options.note: Verse 2 names the specific trouble: slander and deceit.

options.text: A physical illness.
options.note: The psalm names deceitful speech, not sickness, as the trouble.

options.text: Financial poverty.
options.note: The distress is relational and verbal, not financial.

options.text: A coming famine.
options.note: Close in seriousness, but the text specifically names lying lips, not famine.

quiz.q: What image pictures the judgment coming on the deceitful tongue?

options.text: A warrior's sharp arrows and burning coals of the broom tree.
options.note: Verse 4 gives this vivid image of sudden and lasting judgment.

options.text: A gentle rebuke from a friend.
options.note: The image is severe and warlike, not a mild correction.

options.text: A slow fading like grass.
options.note: That image appears elsewhere, in Psalm 129, not here.

options.text: A flood sweeping the land.
options.note: Flood imagery appears in Psalm 124; this psalm uses arrows and coals.

quiz.q: What do Meshech and Kedar represent in this psalm?

options.text: Dwelling among hostile, war loving peoples, far from peace.
options.note: These distant, opposite regions picture the ache of exile among those who hate peace.

options.text: Wealthy trading partners of Israel.
options.note: The emphasis is on hostility and distance from peace, not commerce.

options.text: Close allies who kept covenant with Israel.
options.note: The text laments dwelling among them precisely because they are hostile, not allied.

options.text: Cities within the promised land.
options.note: Both regions lie outside the land, underscoring the psalmist's sense of exile.

quiz.q: What is the psalmist's own stance toward peace, even surrounded by hostility?

options.text: He is for peace, but when he speaks, others want war.
options.note: Verse 7 states this tension plainly.

options.text: He also wants war, matching his enemies.
options.note: The text explicitly says he favors peace, not war.

options.text: He is indifferent to peace or war.
options.note: He actively declares himself for peace, not neutral.

options.text: He seeks peace only after winning by force.
options.note: The psalm shows him desiring peace now, not after conquest.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's cry against lying lips connect to Christ?

options.text: Christ endured false witnesses and did not revile in return, entrusting Himself to God's just judgment.
options.note: 1 Peter 2:23 shows Jesus embodying this pattern at His trial and on the cross.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The pattern of enduring slander while trusting God's justice is directly fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: It predicts the exact words spoken against Jesus.
options.note: The connection is one of pattern and fulfillment, not verbatim prediction.

options.text: It shows Christ retaliating against His accusers.
options.note: Christ notably did not revile in return, the opposite of retaliation.

questions: The psalmist's first instinct in distress is to cry out to the LORD. When trouble comes, is your first move to speak to God, or do you turn there only after trying everything else?
The psalm names a specific pain: lying lips and a deceitful tongue. Where have you been wounded by others' words, and how does it help to know God hears that cry?
The psalmist longs for peace even while living among those who want war. Where are you tempted to answer hostility with hostility rather than continuing to seek peace?

Christ endured false witnesses without reviling in return, entrusting Himself to God who judges justly. What would it look like this week to leave a wrong done to you in God's hands rather than your own?

This is the first step of a long pilgrim road toward Zion. What distant, weary place are you crying out from today, and how does it help to know this is only the beginning of the ascent toward God's presence?

translationNotes.note: The broom tree's coals were known for burning unusually hot and long, making them a fitting image of judgment that is both sudden and lasting.

Meshech and Kedar lie at opposite ends of the ancient world, one north and one south, so the pairing likely functions as a figure of speech for hostile exile in general rather than naming one specific journey.
The phrase rendered I am in favor of peace can also be read I am peace itself, intensifying the contrast with those around him who want war.
